nameStory: This tiny organism gets its name from the Greek words 'stauros' meaning cross and 'astrum' meaning star, referring to its distinctive star-like or cross-shaped appearance when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'orbiculare' means circular, describing its rounded overall form that resembles a miniature geometric ornament.
description: Staurastrum orbiculare is a microscopic single-celled green algae that lives in freshwater environments. This tiny organism is so small you'd need a microscope to see it properly - each cell is only about 20-40 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). It has a distinctive star or cross-like shape with symmetrical arms radiating from a central body, and like other green algae, it makes its own food through photosynthesis. Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these little organisms can be quite abundant in clean ponds and lakes.

idTips.label: Star-shaped form
idTips.description: Under a microscope, the cell appears as a perfect star or cross with symmetrical arms extending from a rounded central body

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny at 20-40 micrometers - you'll only see green specks or cloudiness in water with the naked eye

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vibrant emerald green due to chlorophyll, similar to the color of fresh grass

idTips.label: Clean water indicator
idTips.description: Found in clear, unpolluted freshwater - if the water smells clean and looks crystal clear, you're more likely to find them

habitat: This microscopic algae thrives in clean, nutrient-poor freshwater environments throughout New England, including pristine mountain ponds, clear lakes, and slow-moving streams. You'll find them in waters with good oxygen levels and minimal pollution, often in association with other desmid algae and aquatic plants. They prefer slightly acidic to neutral water conditions and are particularly common in the cleaner lakes of Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine's wilderness areas.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. Best time to collect samples as spring meltwater creates ideal clean conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when photosynthesis is most active. Water samples will show highest concentrations of these green microorganisms.
seasonality.fall: Numbers remain steady through early autumn but begin declining as temperatures drop. Still easily observable in microscope samples.
seasonality.winter: Populations drop significantly under ice cover, though some individuals persist in deeper waters. Difficult to find and collect during frozen periods.

funFact: These tiny organisms are like living water quality test strips - their presence indicates exceptionally clean water, and scientists use them as biological indicators to assess whether a lake or pond is healthy enough to support sensitive aquatic life!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other star-shaped desmids in the same genus, but Staurastrum orbiculare's perfectly circular central body and symmetrical short arms distinguish it from spikier relatives like S. longispinum or more angular species like S. tetracerum.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'algae,' these organisms are quite different from the slimy green algae most people know - they're actually closer to plants in the tree of life and represent some of the most geometrically perfect forms in nature, earning them the nickname 'living crystals' among microscopists.
compareHints: Compared to its Staurastrum relatives, S. orbiculare has a notably rounded, circular central body rather than angular or elongated forms. While species like S. longispinum have long spiky projections and S. tetracerum appears more squared off, S. orbiculare maintains perfect radial symmetry with shorter, more proportioned arms extending from its spherical center.
